In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
14,15 and 5, 6 EETs increase endothelial permeability via Ca2+ dependent mechanisms, whereas 8, 9 and 11, 12 EETs do not.
EETs may play a role in the regulation of endothelial function, although the precise mechanism is not yet known.
EETs are involved in regulation of EC permeability in the isolated perfused rat lung, but the mechanism of EET-induced EC injury is not dependent on depletion of endoplamic reticulum Ca2+ stores.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the role of EETs as a soluble factor linking store depletion and store-dependent Ca(2+) signaling is not supported by our data.
EETs are not involved in regulation of endothelium permeability in isolated rat lungs.
EETs are a heterogeneous family of signaling molecules with respect to regulation of endothelial barrier function in the isolated perfused rat lung.
The main takeaway from our work is that
EETs are not the sole soluble factor linking store-dependent Ca(2+) influx and EC permeability.
EETs are not involved in store-dependent EC permeability in rat lungs.
